In [[mathematics]], '''Kuratowski convergence''' or '''Painlevé-Kuratowski convergence''' is a notion of [[Limit of a sequence|convergence]] for [[subset]]s of a [[topological space]]. First introduced by [[Paul Painlevé]] in lectures on [[mathematical analysis]] in 1902,<ref name=":0">This is reported in the Commentary section of Chapter 4 of Rockafellar and Wets' text.</ref> the concept was popularized in texts by [[Felix Hausdorff]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hausdorff |first=Felix |title=Mengenlehre |publisher=[[Walter de Gruyter & Co.]] |year=1927 |edition=2nd |location=Berlin |language=de}}</ref> and [[Kazimierz Kuratowski]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kuratowski |first=Kazimierz |title=Topologie, I & II |publisher=Panstowowe Wyd Nauk |year=1933 |location=Warsaw |language=fr}}</ref>  Intuitively, the Kuratowski limit of a sequence of sets is where the sets "[[limit point|accumulate]]".

== Definitions ==
For a given sequence <math>\{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> of points in a space <math>X</math>, a [[Accumulation point|limit point]] of the sequence can be understood as any point <math>x \in X</math> where the sequence ''eventually'' becomes arbitrarily close to <math>x</math>. On the other hand, a cluster point of the sequence can be thought of as a point <math>x \in X</math> where the sequence ''frequently'' becomes arbitrarily close to <math>x</math>. The Kuratowski limits inferior and superior generalize this intuition of limit and cluster points to subsets of the given space <math>X</math>.

=== Metric Spaces ===

Let <math>(X,d)</math> be a [[metric space]], where <math>X</math> is a given set. For any point <math>x</math> and any [[non-empty]] subset <math>A \subset X</math>, define the distance between the point and the subset:

:<math>d(x, A) := \inf_{y \in A} d(x, y), \qquad x \in X.</math>

For any sequence of subsets <math>\{A_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> of <math>X</math>, the ''Kuratowski [[limit inferior]]'' (or ''lower closed limit'') of <math>A_n</math> as <math>n \to \infty</math>; is<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_{n} :=&
\left\{ x \in X : \begin{matrix} \mbox{for all open neighbourhoods } U \mbox{ of } x,  U \cap A_{n} \neq \varnothing \mbox{ for large enough } n \end{matrix} \right\} \\
=&\left\{ x \in X : \limsup_{n \to \infty} d(x, A_{n}) = 0 \right\};
\end{align}</math>the ''Kuratowski limit superior'' (or ''upper closed limit'') of <math>A_n</math> as <math>n \to \infty</math>; is<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_{n} :=&
\left\{ x \in X : \begin{matrix} \mbox{for all open neighbourhoods } U \mbox{ of } x, U \cap A_{n} \neq \varnothing \mbox{ for infinitely many } n \end{matrix} \right\} \\
=&\left\{ x \in X : \liminf_{n \to \infty} d(x, A_{n}) = 0 \right\};
\end{align}</math>If the Kuratowski limits inferior and superior agree, then the common set is called the ''Kuratowski limit'' of <math>A_n</math> and is denoted <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}}_{n \to \infty} A_n</math>.

=== Topological Spaces ===

If <math display="inline">(X, \tau)</math> is a [[topological space]], and <math display="inline">\{A_i\}_{i \in I}</math> are a [[Net (mathematics)|net]] of subsets of <math display="inline">X</math>, the limits inferior and superior follow a similar construction. For a given point <math display="inline">x \in X</math> denote <math display="inline">\mathcal{N}(x)</math> the collection of [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|open neighborhoods]] of <math display="inline">x</math>. The ''Kuratowski limit inferior'' of <math display="inline">\{A_i\}_{i \in I}</math> is the set<math display="block">\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_i := \left\{
    x \in X :
    \forall U \in \mathcal{N}(x) \, \exists i_0 \in I \colon \forall i \geq i_0 \Rightarrow U \cap A_i \neq \varnothing
\right\},</math>and the ''Kuratowski limit superior'' is the set<math display="block">\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_i := \left\{
    x \in X :
    \forall U \in \mathcal{N}(x) \, \forall i_0 \in I \, \exists i \geq i_0 \colon U \cap A_i \neq \varnothing
\right\}.</math>Elements of <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_i</math> are called ''limit points'' of <math display="inline">\{A_i\}_{i \in I}</math> and elements of <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_i</math> are called ''cluster points'' of <math display="inline">\{A_i\}_{i \in I}</math>. In other words, <math>x</math> is a limit point of <math display="inline">\{A_i\}_{i \in I}</math> if each of its neighborhoods intersects <math>A_i</math> for all <math>i</math> in a "residual" subset of <math>I</math>, while <math>x</math> is a cluster point of <math display="inline">\{A_i\}_{i \in I}</math> if each of its neighborhoods intersects <math>A_i</math> for all <math>i</math> in a [[Cofinal (mathematics)|cofinal]] subset of <math>I</math>.

When these sets agree, the common set is the ''Kuratowski limit'' of <math display="inline">\{A_i\}_{i \in I}</math>, denoted <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_i</math>.

== Examples ==

* Suppose <math>(X, d)</math> is [[Separable space|separable]] where <math>X</math> is a [[Perfect set|perfect]] set, and let <math>D = \{d_1, d_2, \dots\}</math> be an enumeration of a [[Countable set|countable]] [[Dense set|dense]] subset of <math>X</math>. Then the sequence <math>\{A_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> defined by <math>A_n := \{d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n\}</math> has <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n = X</math>.
* Given two closed subsets <math>B, C \subset X</math>, defining <math>A_{2n-1} := B</math> and <math>A_{2n} := C</math> for each <math>n=1,2,\dots</math> yields <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_n = B \cap C</math> and <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_n = B \cup C</math>.
* The sequence of [[Metric space#The topology of a metric space|closed balls]] <math>A_n := \{y \in X: d(x_n,y) \leq r_n\}</math>converges in the sense of Kuratowski when <math>x_n \to x</math> in <math>X</math> and <math>r_n \to r</math> in <math>[0, +\infty)</math>, and in particular, <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}}(A_n) = \{y \in X : d(x,y) \leq r\}</math>. If <math>r_n \to +\infty</math>, then <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n = X</math> while <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}}(X \setminus A_n) = \emptyset</math>.
* Let <math display="inline">A_{n} := \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : \sin (n x) = 0 \}</math>. Then <math>A_n</math> converges in the Kuratowski sense to the entire line.
* In a [[topological vector space]], if <math>\{A_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> is a sequence of [[Convex cone|cones]], then so are the Kuratowski limits superior and inferior. For example, the sets <math>A_n := \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : y \geq n|x|\}</math> converge to <math>\{(0,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : y \geq 0\}</math>.

== Properties ==

The following properties hold for the limits inferior and superior in both the metric and topological contexts, but are stated in the metric formulation for ease of reading.<ref>The interested reader may consult Beer's text, in particular Chapter 5, Section 2, for these and more technical results in the topological setting. For Euclidean spaces, Rockafellar and Wets report similar facts in Chapter 4.</ref>
* Both <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_n</math> and <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_n</math> are closed subsets of <math>X</math>, and <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_n \subset \mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_n</math> always holds.
* The upper and lower limits do not distinguish between sets and their [[Closure (mathematics)|closures]]: <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_n = \mathop{\mathrm{Li}} \mathop{\mathrm{cl}}(A_n)</math> and <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_n = \mathop{\mathrm{L s}} \mathop{\mathrm{cl}}(A_n)</math>.
* If <math>A_n := A</math> is a constant sequence, then <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n = \mathop{\mathrm{cl}} A</math>.
* If <math>
A_n := \{x_n\}
</math> is a sequence of singletons, then <math>
\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_n
</math> and <math>
\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_n
</math> consist of the limit points and cluster points, respectively, of the sequence <math>
\{x_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty} \subset X
</math>.
* If <math>A_n \subset B_n \subset C_n</math> and <math>B := \mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n = \mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} C_n</math>, then <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} B_n = B</math>.
* (''Hit and miss criteria'') For a closed subset <math>A \subset X</math>, one has
** <math>A \subset \mathop{\mathrm{Li}} A_n</math>, if and only if for every open set <math>U \subset X</math> with <math>A \cap U \ne \emptyset</math> there exists <math>n_0</math> such that <math>A_n \cap U \ne \emptyset</math> for all <math>n_0 \leq n</math>,
** <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} A_n \subset A</math>, if and only if for every compact set <math>K \subset X</math> with <math>A \cap K = \emptyset</math> there exists <math>n_0</math> such that <math>A_n \cap K = \emptyset</math> for all <math>n_0 \leq n</math>.
*If <math>A_1 \subset A_2 \subset A_3 \subset \cdots</math> then the Kuratowski limit exists, and <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n = \mathop{\mathrm{cl}} \left( \bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty} A_n \right)</math>. Conversely, if <math>A_1 \supset A_2 \supset A_3 \supset \cdots</math> then the Kuratowski limit exists, and <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n = \bigcap_{n = 1}^{\infty} \mathop{\mathrm{cl}}(A_n)</math>.
*If <math>d_H</math> denotes [[Hausdorff metric]], then <math>d_H(A_n, A) \to 0</math> implies <math>\mathop{\mathrm{cl}}A = \mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n</math>. However, noncompact closed sets may converge in the sense of Kuratowski while <math>d_H(A_n, \mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} A_n) = +\infty</math> for each <math>n=1,2,\dots</math><ref>For an example, consider the sequence of cones in the previous section.</ref>
*Convergence in the sense of Kuratowski is weaker than convergence in the sense of [[Vietoris topology|Vietoris]] but equivalent to convergence in the sense of Fell. If <math>X</math> is compact, then these are all equivalent and agree with convergence in Hausdorff metric.

== Kuratowski Continuity of Set-Valued Functions ==
Let <math>S : X \rightrightarrows Y</math> be a set-valued function between the spaces <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>; namely, <math>S(x) \in Y</math> for all <math>x \in X</math>. Denote <math>S^{-1}(y) = \{x \in X : y \in S(x)\}</math>. We can define the operators<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathop{\mathrm{Li}}_{x' \to x} S(x') :=& \bigcap_{x' \to x} \mathop{\mathrm{Li}} S(x'), \qquad x \in X \\
\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}}_{x' \to x} S(x') :=& \bigcup_{x' \to x} \mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} S(x'), \qquad x \in X\\
\end{align}</math>where <math>x' \to x</math> means convergence in sequences when <math>X</math> is metrizable and convergence in nets otherwise. Then,

* <math>S</math> is ''inner semi-continuous'' at <math>x \in X</math> if <math display="inline">S(x) \subset \mathop{\mathrm{Li}}_{x' \to x} S(x')</math>;
* <math>S</math> is ''outer semi-continuous'' at <math>x \in X</math> if <math display="inline">\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}}_{x' \to x} S(x') \subset S(x)</math>.

When <math>S</math> is both inner and outer semi-continuous at <math>x \in X</math>, we say that <math>S</math> is ''continuous'' (or continuous ''in the sense of Kuratowski'').

Continuity of set-valued functions is commonly defined in terms of [[Hemicontinuity|lower- and upper-hemicontinuity]] popularized by [[Claude Berge|Berge]].<ref>Rockafellar and Wets write in the Commentary to Chapter 6 of their text: "The terminology of 'inner' and 'outer' semicontinuity, instead of 'lower' and 'upper', has been forced on us by the fact that the prevailing definition of 'upper semicontinuity' in the literature is out of step with developments in set convergence and the scope of applications that must be handled, now that mappings <math>S</math> with unbounded range and even unbounded value sets <math>S(x)</math> are so important... Despite the historical justification, the tide can no longer be turned in the meaning of 'upper semicontinuity', yet the concept of 'continuity' is too crucial for applications to be left in the poorly usable form that rests on such an unfortunately restrictive property [of upper semicontinuity]"; see pages 192-193. Note also that authors differ on whether "semi-continuity" or "hemi-continuity" is the preferred language for Vietoris-Berge continuity concepts.</ref> In this sense, a set-valued function is continuous if and only if the function <math>f_S : X \to 2^Y</math> defined by <math>f(x) = S(x)</math> is continuous with respect to the [[Vietoris topology|Vietoris]] hyperspace topology of <math>2^Y</math>. For set-valued functions with closed values, continuity in the sense of Vietoris-Berge is stronger than continuity in the sense of Kuratowski.

=== Examples ===

* The set-valued function <math>B(x,r) = \{y \in X : d(x,y) \leq r \}</math> is continuous <math>X \times [0,+\infty) \rightrightarrows X</math>.
* Given a function <math>f : X \to [-\infty, +\infty]</math>, the superlevel set mapping <math>S_f(x) := \{\lambda \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) \leq \lambda\}</math> is outer semi-continuous at <math>x</math>, if and only if <math>f</math> is lower semi-continuous at <math>x</math>. Similarly, <math>S_f</math> is inner semi-continuous at <math>x</math>, if and only if <math>f</math> is upper semi-continuous at <math>x</math>.

=== Properties ===

* If <math>S</math> is continuous at <math>x</math>, then <math>S(x)</math> is closed.
* <math>S</math> is outer semi-continuous at <math>x</math>, if and only if for every <math>y \notin S(x)</math> there are neighborhoods <math>V \in \mathcal{N}(y)</math> and <math>U \in \mathcal{N}(x)</math> such that <math>U \cap S^{-1}(V) = \emptyset</math>.
* <math>S</math> is inner semi-continuous at <math>x</math>, if and only if for every <math>y \in S(x)</math> and neighborhood <math>V \in \mathcal{N}(y)</math> there is a neighborhood <math>U \in \mathcal{N}(x)</math> such that <math>V \cap S(x') \ne \emptyset</math> for all <math>x' \in U</math>.
* <math>S</math> is (globally) outer semi-continuous, if and only if its graph <math>\{(x,y) \in X \times Y : y \in S(x)\}</math> is closed.
* (''Relations to Vietoris-Berge continuity''). Suppose <math>S(x)</math> is closed.
** <math>S</math> is inner semi-continuous at <math>x</math>, if and only if <math>S</math> is [[Lower hemicontinuous|lower hemi-continuous]] at <math>x</math> in the sense of Vietoris-Berge.
** If <math>S</math> is [[Upper hemicontinuous|upper hemi-continuous]] at <math>x</math>, then <math>S</math> is outer semi-continuous at <math>x</math>. The converse is false in general, but holds when <math>Y</math> is a compact space.
* If <math>S : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m</math>has a convex graph, then <math>S</math> is inner semi-continuous at each point of the interior of the domain of <math>S</math>. Conversely, given any inner semi-continuous set-valued function <math>S</math>, the convex hull mapping <math>T(x) := \mathop{\mathrm{conv}} S(x)</math> is also inner semi-continuous.

== Epi-convergence and Γ-convergence ==
{{Main|Epi-convergence|Γ-convergence}}
For the metric space <math>
(X, d)
</math> a sequence of functions <math>f_n : X \to [-\infty, +\infty]</math>, the ''epi-limit inferior'' (or ''lower epi-limit'') is the function <math>\mathop{\mathrm{e}\liminf} f_n</math> defined by the [[Epigraph (mathematics)|epigraph]] equation<math display="block">
\mathop{\mathrm{epi}} \left( \mathop{\mathrm{e}\liminf} f_n\right) := \mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} \left(\mathop{\mathrm{epi}} f_n\right),
</math>and similarly the ''epi-limit superior'' (or ''upper epi-limit'') is the function <math>\mathop{\mathrm{e}\limsup} f_n</math> defined by the epigraph equation<math display="block">
\mathop{\mathrm{epi}} \left( \mathop{\mathrm{e}\limsup} f_n\right)
:= \mathop{\mathrm{Li}} \left(\mathop{\mathrm{epi}} f_n\right).
</math>Since Kuratowski upper and lower limits are closed sets, it follows that both <math>\mathop{\mathrm{e}\liminf} f_n</math> and <math>\mathop{\mathrm{e}\limsup} f_n</math> are [[Semi-continuity|lower semi-continuous]] functions. Similarly, since <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Li}} \mathop{\mathrm{epi}} f_n \subset
\mathop{\mathrm{Ls}} \mathop{\mathrm{epi}} f_n</math>, it follows that <math>\mathop{\mathrm{e}\liminf} f_n \leq \mathop{\mathrm{e}\liminf} f_n</math> uniformly. These functions agree, if and only if <math>\mathop{\mathrm{Lim}} \mathop{\mathrm{epi}} f_n</math> exists, and the associated function is called the ''epi-limit'' of <math>\{f_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}</math>.

When <math>(X, \tau)</math> is a topological space, epi-convergence of the sequence <math>\{f_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> is called Γ-convergence. From the perspective of Kuratowski convergence there is no distinction between epi-limits and Γ-limits. The concepts are usually studied separately, because epi-convergence admits special characterizations that rely on the metric space structure of <math>X</math>, which does not hold in topological spaces generally.
